title: Goldfield Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Goldfield well depths center at 300 feet, with typical completed-well costs of $25,500-$42,000 in fractured mountain bedrock.
h1: Goldfield, Colorado Well Depths, Yields and Costs
intro_html:
Goldfield sits in fractured mountain bedrock, where well results can change substantially from one lot to the next. Records within five miles show 621 permitted wells, but only 359 report a total depth and 169 report a pump yield. That means the local data is useful for setting expectations, not for guaranteeing what a new well will produce.

The practical starting point is a median drilled depth of 300 feet and a median reported yield of 7.0 gallons per minute. Nearby Victor, Cripple Creek and Midland provide useful comparison points when checking properties, but the well permits closest to the lot matter most.

sections.heading: Goldfield well depth: plan for hard, variable drilling
sections.html:
Goldfield wells have a median depth of 300 feet. The middle half runs from 140 to 440 feet, so a driller’s bid based only on the median can miss the actual ground conditions. About 22% of recorded wells are under 100 feet, 26% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 41% from 300 to 600 feet, and 11% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 3,140 feet.

Most permits identify unnamed fractured bedrock, with 597 wells in that category and 8 identified as Fractured Granite. Granite and gneiss commonly produce water through fractures rather than a uniform underground layer. For a buyer, nearby well depths are more useful than a countywide assumption. Ask for several permits on the same ridge, drainage or road before accepting a drilling allowance.

sections.heading: Expected well yield around Goldfield
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 2.0 and 9.1 gallons per minute. The yield mix is fairly broad: 8% of reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, 31% produce from 1 to 5, 54% produce from 5 to 15, and 7% produce more than 15 gallons per minute.

For a household buyer, a 7.0-gallon-per-minute result is generally a workable planning figure, but it is not a promise for an individual lot. The 8% under 1 gallon per minute deserves attention because a low-producing well may require storage and careful demand management. Confirm the permitted use, pump test, storage tank size and actual recovery before relying on the well for a larger home or additional fixtures.

sections.heading: Water levels and the recent Goldfield trend
sections.html:
Among the 46 records reporting a static water level, the median depth to water is 100 feet, and the middle half runs from 58 to 172 feet below the surface. A static level is measured when the well is not being pumped. It is not the same as the pumping level, and it does not tell you by itself how quickly the well recovers.

The decade figures show a higher reported water level depth in the newer records: the median was 100 feet below ground in the 2010s and 135 feet in the 2020s. That change suggests water was measured deeper in the more recent sample, but the dataset is small and may reflect different locations, seasons or measurement conditions. Have the current owner provide recent pump and water-level information rather than assuming the older permit value still applies.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Goldfield, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity is spread across several decades. The records show 22 permits from the 1970s, 54 from the 1980s, 153 from the 1990s, 199 from the 2000s, 84 from the 2010s and 68 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. Domestic or household wells make up 63% of the use mix, while stock wells account for 8%, monitoring wells for 30% and irrigation wells for 0%.

The most active driller listed is Mountain Well Improvement LLC, associated with Wiley, David D., with 147 records. Authorized (PE, PG) appears on 125 records, and Black Mountain Drilling, associated with Schnoes, Adam J., appears on 50. These are permit-record associations, not a recommendation. Check the actual well construction report, casing, grout, pump test and final permit status before comparing contractors.

sections.heading: What a new well costs in Goldfield
sections.html:
Goldfield drilling is priced around fractured mountain bedrock, described in the local cost model as granite and gneiss. The typical drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 300-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $19,500 to $30,000.

A finished well, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical work, is modeled at about $25,500 to $42,000 at that depth. Treat that as a planning range, not a fixed bid. The 140-to-440-foot middle-half depth range shows why the final price can move substantially. Ask each driller what is included, how additional footage is charged, and whether casing, grout, permitting, pump installation, storage and electrical connections are separate line items.

sections.heading: Goldfield risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
Low yield is the first practical risk. Eight percent of reported wells produce under 1 gallon per minute, and fractured-bedrock wells can also encounter dry holes or changing production between nearby lots. A buyer should review the well construction report, pump test, static and pumping levels, and any storage system. Confirm that the permit allows the intended household use; an exempt household-use well is not automatically suitable for every proposed use.

Water quality also deserves a site-specific review. Within about ten miles, the mapping shows 9 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 443 historic mine features and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped features do not prove contamination at a particular well. Test the water before closing and consider a location-specific review of mines, septic setbacks, drainage and neighboring wells. Colorado DWR permit records help with construction history, but they are not a substitute for laboratory testing.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a Goldfield lot
sections.html:
Before buying, gather permits for neighboring wells in Goldfield, Victor, Cripple Creek and the surrounding roads, then compare depths, yields, water levels and uses. Give the driller the parcel location and ask for a written estimate that explains the assumed depth and the price if the hole must go deeper. On fractured granite or gneiss, no nearby result can guarantee the next fracture will carry water.

For a building site, confirm the well permit, legal access, septic feasibility, electrical route and trenching distance before finalizing plans. If the basin is over-appropriated, water administration and an augmentation plan may affect new uses. Colorado’s exempt-well pumping limit is 35 gallons per minute, but the permit’s actual conditions control. A water test, septic evaluation and current well inspection are inexpensive compared with discovering a problem after closing.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Goldfield, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth near Goldfield is 300 feet. The middle half runs from 140 to 440 feet, while 41% of wells are between 300 and 600 feet. Some are much deeper: the deepest record is 3,140 feet. Because the area is fractured mountain bedrock, nearby permits are more useful than the median alone when estimating a new well.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Goldfield?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured granite and gneiss. At the 300-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $19,500 to $30,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical work is estimated at $25,500 to $42,000. Greater depth, casing and difficult access can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Goldfield?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 2.0 to 9.1 gallons per minute. About 8% of reported wells produce under 1 gallon per minute, while 54% produce from 5 to 15. These are permit-record results, not guarantees. Review the actual pump test and recovery information for the property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Goldfield?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that a particular well is safe to drink. The area within about ten miles includes 9 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 443 historic mine features and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped features do not prove contamination at your property, but they support testing the well water through a qualified laboratory before closing.

faq.q: Are Goldfield well water levels getting lower?
faq.a: The reported median static water level was 100 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 135 feet in the 2020s. That indicates deeper measured water levels in the newer sample, but only 46 records report static water levels. Different locations, seasons and measurement methods may affect the comparison. Obtain a current water-level check instead of relying only on an older permit.
